source.title: REPAIR: REnormalizing Permuted Activations for Interpolation Repair
source.authors: Keller Jordan; Hanie Sedghi; O. Saukh; R. Entezari; Behnam Neyshabur

record.tranche_reason: The study reports activation-correlation and filter-similarity observations for independently trained, aligned networks. These are a different measure from the claim’s cross-model distance geometry, but bear on whether independently trained networks learn similar features.
record.gate_note: The reported interpolation barriers, accuracy changes after REPAIR, and width/depth sweeps measure weight-space interpolation performance, not representational similarity, so they are not rows for these claim versions. Cited findings from other studies are also excluded.
record.test_reason: A weak, incidental test of V3. The paper is mainly about weight-space interpolation with REPAIR, using neuron alignment (Li et al. 2015) as a tool. It does report two observations on cross-seed feature similarity: typical matched-unit correlation of about 0.4 (Sec 3.2), and a qualitative ResNet50 first-layer filter comparison (Fig 9). Interpolation barriers do not measure representational similarity.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. Neuron alignment alone is insufficient for low-barrier interpolation because of variance collapse. REPAIR rescales preactivations and largely removes barriers (ResNet50/ImageNet midpoint from below 1% to 56.5% accuracy), giving partial support to Entezari's conjecture. However, this requires leaving strictly permuted interpolation, unless LayerNorm is used.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses activation-based neuron alignment as part of weight-space interpolation experiments and reports limited feature-similarity observations; it does not directly test representational convergence as a function of scale or performance.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper notes that paired-unit correlations are typically imperfect; its broader interpolation results vary with architecture, normalization, width, depth, and whether REPAIR is applied, but those results do not measure the claim’s representational similarity.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear interpolation between permutation-aligned, independently trained networks suffers variance collapse. REPAIR reduces barriers by 60-100% across architectures, and barriers shrink with width.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Independently trained networks are linearly mode-connected modulo permutation (Entezari conjecture); this is a weight-space claim, not a representational one.

record.problems: The claim-relevant evidence is limited: the correlation estimate has no stated sample size or uncertainty, and the ResNet50 filter comparison is qualitative and concerns only the first layer of one model pair.
record.rows_left_out: No other claim-relevant rows identified. Interpolation performance results were left out because they measure loss or accuracy along weight-space paths, not representational similarity.

untested.parts: All: no comparison across scale, capability, architectures, objectives or data.
Shared subspaces, the fraction of shared features, layers beyond the first, and multiple seed pairs.
Representation mapping, stitching or relative representations. Weight interpolation barriers are not representation maps.
All: no interpretable feature or circuit recurrence across models.
All: no variation of similarity metric or inputs.
All: no plateau or shared-data explanation tested.

record.verdict_notes: The paper cites Li et al. 2015 (an original source) only as the alignment method; it is not itself an original source. Its evidence on V3 is thin and incidental. A case could be made for T4 (uses alignment as a tool), but the corr ≈ 0.4 statement and Fig 9 are its own observations on cross-seed feature sharing, so it is kept as a weak T2 test of V3.

versions.untested_parts: Whether representational alignment rises with model size or capability across different architectures, objectives, data, or modalities.
Alignment between vision and language representations of paired images and captions as model performance changes.

The study reports limited observations on aligned units and first-layer filters, but does not establish how many features are shared across a broad set of seeds, layers, or models, or test shared subspaces.
Mapping one model’s representations onto another’s, including linear maps, stitching, relative representations, or unpaired mappings.
Recurrence of interpretable features or circuits such as neurons or SAE features.
Whether representational convergence depends on similarity metric settings or input distribution.
Whether representational alignment plateaus or is explained by shared data or objectives rather than a common model of reality.

rows.subject: paired aligned endpoint networks (architecture not stated for this statistic)
rows.operation_detail: Reports correlation between activation-matched units in independently trained networks.
rows.value: corr(X1, X2)≈0.4 for typical aligned pairs
rows.note: The paper says aligned pairs are typically not perfectly correlated; it does not state the number of pairs or networks behind this estimate.
rows.check: The value is a stated 'typical' figure with no architecture, layer, data or sample size, offered to motivate the variance-collapse calculation. Treat it as a heuristic, not a measured result. The baseline should be perfect alignment (corr = 1), which the paper names as the same-features case.

source_check.correct: State: cannot_determine for V3. The approximately 0.4 correlation is a stated typical value motivating a variance calculation, without a documented measurement protocol or control. It does not determine how many features or subspaces are shared.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2, pp. 5–6, immediately before and after the midpoint-variance calculation.
source_check.problem: The row presents a heuristic typical value as a measurement and treats imperfect unit correspondence as partial V3, although V3 permits different units and bases.

rows.subject: ResNet50 models A and B
rows.operation_detail: Visually compares first-layer filters after permuting model B to maximize activation-wise correlation with model A.
rows.baseline: model B filters in their original positions
rows.value: Some paired filters appear nearly identical; others have no close match.
rows.note: A qualitative observation for the first layer of one pair of independently trained models; the paper does not quantify the fraction of close matches.
rows.check: Qualitative only: one ResNet50 pair on ImageNet, first layer only. 'Some nearly identical, others no close match' is what V3 describes (shared features but not all units), so observed fits better than partial.

relationships.condition: ResNet50 pair independently trained on ImageNet, first-layer filters
relationships.reason: After activation-correlation permutation, some paired filters look nearly identical while others have no match, as V3 describes (R2).
relationships.display_finding: Activation-correlation matching paired some nearly identical first-layer filters, while other filters lacked counterparts.

relation.reason: Figure 9 reports the study's own cross-seed filter comparison bearing on V3, beyond using alignment solely as a tool.

tranche.reason: The interpolation and variance-collapse investigation supplies incidental evidence about cross-seed feature correspondence, including the study's own aligned-filter comparison.

source_check.notes: The authors-conclusion paraphrase is broadly accurate, although substantial ImageNet interpolation barriers remain after REPAIR. Figure 9 is qualitative evidence from one model pair and its first layer; it gives no fraction of matching filters.

statements.correction: Section 3.2: typical aligned-unit correlation approximately 0.4; architecture, dataset, sample size and uncertainty unspecified for that statistic. Sections 5.1 and 5.3: ResNet20 width sweeps measure interpolation barriers. No trained-versus-random permutation-correlation comparison or correlation-versus-width result reported.
statements.problem: The approximately 0.4 typical correlation and missing measurement details are supported. The trained-versus-random ResNet20 permutation-correlation comparison, constant correlation with width, and associated width/reset conditions are not reported in this study.
